rows.selection_reason: No experiments have been completed, so the highest-priority task is to establish a clean, interpretable baseline. config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) is the simplest and most standard configuration: RNA is the primary modality in cellular profiling, PCA is the most widely used and interpretable dimensionality-reduction encoder, and singleprofile is the minimal profile setting. This experiment will give a reference validation accuracy/F1 for the RNA-only, single-profile case. Every subsequent experiment—image-only baselines, multiprofile variants, alternative encoders (scvi, scgpt), and multimodal fusion—can be meaningfully compared against this anchor. Without this baseline, performance differences from more complex configurations would be uninterpretable. Under a limited budget, spending the first experiment on the simplest, most informative baseline maximizes the information gained per experiment and sets the stage for efficient exploration of the remaining design dimensions.

With only one completed experiment (config_001: rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000 → acc 0.485), evidence is extremely sparse. The most critical open question for a multimodal cellular profiling study is whether adding an image modality to the RNA baseline actually improves performance. config_016 (multimodal, singleprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, concat) is the most direct, controlled extension of config_001: it holds the RNA encoder and profile setting constant while introducing the image modality with the simplest standard fusion (concat). This single experiment will (a) establish whether multimodal integration is worthwhile at all, (b) provide a multimodal baseline against which to later compare fusion strategies, image encoders, and profile settings, and (c) reduce the largest source of uncertainty in the design space. If multimodal helps, we exploit that direction; if not, we efficiently rule out an entire branch of the search. No other single experiment reduces uncertainty about this fundamental design choice as cleanly.

With only two completed experiments, the evidence is very sparse. config_016 (multimodal, resnet50, concat) outperforms config_001 (RNA-only) by ~4.2% accuracy, but we cannot yet determine whether this gain comes from the image modality alone or from the synergistic combination of both modalities. config_010 (image_only, singleprofile, resnet50) is the critical ablation: it isolates the image contribution using the same encoder and profile setting as config_016. If image-only approaches or exceeds the multimodal result, the RNA channel adds little value and future budget should focus on image encoder/architecture choices. If image-only is substantially lower, the fusion is truly synergistic and we should invest in refining fusion strategy and multiprofile aggregation. This single experiment resolves the most fundamental uncertainty in the search space and will most efficiently guide all subsequent decisions under the limited budget.

Evidence: config_016 (multimodal, singleprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, concat) is the current best at 0.527 acc / 0.510 F1, outperforming rna-only (0.485) and far exceeding image-only (0.208). The multiprofile axis is completely untested across all three model settings, representing the largest remaining source of uncertainty. Question: Does aggregating multiple profiles (via avgpool) on top of the best-known multimodal setup yield a meaningful gain over singleprofile? Why this is the best next experiment: config_018 is the minimal, clean extension of the current best (same encoders, same concat fusion) that isolates the multiprofile + avgpool variable. avgpool is chosen over transformer to keep the aggregation simple and reduce overfitting risk with limited data. A positive result would justify investing further in multiprofile configurations (transformer aggregation, other encoders); a null or negative result would efficiently rule out that axis and redirect budget toward image-encoder or RNA-encoder variations. Under a tight budget, resolving this high-impact, unexplored design axis provides the greatest expected information gain per experiment.

Evidence: config_018 (multimodal, multiprofile, PCA, ResNet50, avgpool, concat) achieved 0.619 acc, a large jump over single-profile multimodal (config_016, 0.527) and RNA-only single-profile (config_001, 0.485). This confirms multi-profile aggregation is the dominant performance driver. Uncertainty: we do not yet know whether avgpool is the optimal aggregation strategy or whether a transformer-based aggregation (which can model inter-profile relationships) would further improve performance. config_020 is a clean single-variable change from config_018 (avgpool → transformer, all else identical), directly testing whether more expressive profile aggregation yields gains. This is the best next experiment because it exploits our strongest finding (multi-profile is critical) while resolving a key design-axis uncertainty with minimal confounding, and the result will inform whether to invest further in aggregation complexity or pivot to other dimensions (fusion strategy, encoder quality).

The strongest evidence so far points to config_018 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, concat) at 0.619 acc as the current best, with multiprofile contributing the largest single gain (+0.092 over singleprofile) and avgpool outperforming transformer (+0.04). However, the fusion strategy has only been tested as 'concat' across all multimodal runs. config_019 is the minimal controlled change from the best config—swapping concat for weighted fusion while holding every other factor constant. This directly tests whether the modality combination strategy can be further optimized, which is a high-leverage design choice given that the image modality alone is very weak (0.208) and the multimodal gain over RNA-only is modest (+0.042 in singleprofile). If weighted fusion helps, it is a free improvement; if not, it confirms concat is sufficient and we can redirect budget toward image encoder or RNA encoder upgrades. Under a limited budget, this single-variable test from the best-known configuration is the most information-efficient next step.

Evidence: The dominant signal is clearly RNA (0.485 vs 0.208 for image-only), and the best configuration so far (config_019: multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, weighted, acc=0.639) uses only a linear PCA encoder for RNA. The aggregation (avgpool > transformer) and fusion (weighted > concat) choices are now well-established. The largest unexplored dimension that could move performance is the RNA encoder quality, since RNA drives most of the signal. Question tested: Does replacing PCA with scgpt (a pretrained single-cell foundation model capturing non-linear transcriptomic structure) improve on the current best in the otherwise-identical multimodal/multiprofile/avgpool/weighted setting? Why this is the best next experiment: It isolates exactly one variable (RNA encoder) from the best-performing configuration, so any performance change is attributable to the encoder choice. If scgpt helps, it opens a high-impact axis for further gains; if it does not, we learn PCA is sufficient and can redirect budget toward image encoder or other factors. This is more informative than testing a better image encoder (given image-only is only 0.208) or re-testing aggregation/fusion combinations already shown to be suboptimal.

The current best configuration (config_019: multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, weighted; acc=0.639) establishes that multiprofile + avgpool + weighted fusion is the strongest design so far. However, every multimodal experiment to date has used resnet50 as the image encoder, and the image-only baseline (config_010, resnet50) was very weak (acc=0.208), suggesting resnet50 may not extract sufficiently informative visual features for this task. config_025 tests the same proven architecture (multiprofile, pca_n2000, avgpool, weighted) but swaps in imagenet_vit_l, a substantially stronger image encoder. This is the highest-value next experiment because: (1) it isolates a single, completely unexplored design dimension (image encoder capacity) while holding all other proven-optimal choices fixed, (2) it has high potential upside if ViT-L captures richer morphological features, and (3) it has high information value even if it underperforms, as it would confirm that image encoder choice is not a bottleneck and redirect effort toward other variables. Under a limited budget, this single experiment resolves a major source of uncertainty about whether the current performance ceiling is driven by the image backbone.

Evidence: With concat fusion, avgpool aggregation outperformed transformer by ~4% (0.619 vs 0.579), and weighted fusion outperformed concat by ~2% (0.639 vs 0.619) under avgpool. However, the aggregation×fusion interaction is untested: we do not know whether the avgpool>transformer gap persists when fusion is weighted. Question: Does transformer aggregation remain inferior under weighted fusion, or does weighted fusion partially compensate for the weaker aggregation? Why this is the best next experiment: It is the most direct logical extension of the two strongest findings (avgpool superiority and weighted superiority), it cleanly isolates the aggregation variable in the context of the best-performing fusion strategy, and its result will determine whether transformer can be ruled out entirely for all remaining experiments—saving budget from exploring a potentially dead branch. If transformer+weighted is also clearly worse, we can confidently focus all subsequent experiments on avgpool variants and new encoders; if it is competitive, it reveals an important interaction that changes the search strategy.

Evidence: The current best (config_019: multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, weighted; acc=0.639) establishes that multiprofile + avgpool + weighted fusion is the strongest architecture. Among RNA encoders, pca_n2000 (0.639) far outperforms scgpt (0.525), but scvi_n200 remains completely untested in the multimodal multiprofile setting. Uncertainty: It is unclear whether a variational autoencoder (scvi), which learns a nonlinear latent representation of single-cell data, can match or exceed the linear PCA projection. scgpt's poor performance suggests learned encoders may struggle here, but scvi is architecturally distinct (VAE vs. generative transformer) and its behavior is genuinely unknown. What this tests: config_031 isolates the RNA encoder as the sole variable from the current best, directly measuring whether scvi_n200 can compete with pca_n2000 under the best-known aggregation/fusion regime. Why it is the best next experiment: It resolves the most important remaining design uncertainty (RNA encoder choice) with a single clean comparison, and the outcome will either confirm PCA as the optimal encoder (closing that search axis) or reveal a new promising direction—maximizing information gained per experiment under the limited budget.
